{{short description|Finite field of two elements}}

{{math|GF(2)}} (also denoted <math>\mathbb F_2</math>, {{math|'''Z'''/2'''Z'''}} or <math>\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z</math>) is the [[finite field]] with two elements.<ref>{{cite book | zbl=0866.11069 | last1=Lidl | first1=Rudolf | last2=Niederreiter | first2=Harald | author2-link=Harald Niederreiter | title=Finite fields | edition=2nd | series=Encyclopedia of Mathematics and Its Applications | volume=20 | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | year=1997 | isbn=0-521-39231-4 | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/finitefields0000lidl_a8r3 }}</ref>{{efn|GF is the [[initialism]] of ''Galois field'', another name for finite fields.}} 

{{math|GF(2)}} is the [[Field (mathematics)|field]] with the smallest possible number of elements, and is unique if the [[additive identity]] and the [[multiplicative identity]] are denoted respectively {{val|0}} and {{val|1}}, as usual.

The elements of {{math|GF(2)}} may be identified with the two possible values of a [[bit]] and to the [[Boolean domain|Boolean value]]s ''true'' and ''false''. It follows that {{math|GF(2)}} is fundamental and ubiquitous in [[computer science]] and its [[mathematical logic|logical]] foundations.

== Definition ==
GF(2) is the unique field with two elements. Its [[additive identity|additive]] and [[multiplicative identity|multiplicative identities]] are respectively denoted {{val|0}} and {{val|1}}.

Its addition is defined as the usual addition of integers but modulo 2 and corresponds to the table below:

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center; margin: auto;"
|-
! + !! 0 !! 1
|-
! 0
| 0 || 1
|-
! 1
| 1 || 0
|}

If the elements of GF(2) are seen as Boolean values, then the addition is the same as that of the [[logical XOR]] operation.
Since each element equals its [[opposite (mathematics)|opposite]], subtraction is thus the same operation as addition.

The multiplication of GF(2) is the usual multiplication (see the table below), and on Boolean variables corresponds to the [[logical AND]] operation.

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center; margin: auto;"
|-
! × !! 0 !! 1
|-
! 0
| 0 || 0
|-
! 1
| 0 || 1
|}

GF(2) can be identified with the field of the [[integers modulo a prime|integers modulo {{val|2}}]], that is, the [[quotient ring]] of the [[ring of integers]] '''Z''' by the [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] 2'''Z''' of all [[even number]]s: {{nowrap|1=GF(2) = '''Z'''/2'''Z'''}}.

Notations {{math|'''Z'''{{sub|2}}}} and <math>\mathbb Z_2</math> may be encountered although they can be confused with the notation of [[p-adic integer|{{val|2}}-adic integers]].

== Properties ==
{{main|finite field}}
Because GF(2) is a field, many of the familiar properties of number systems such as the [[rational number]]s and [[real number]]s are retained:

* addition has an [[identity element]] (0) and an inverse for every element;
* multiplication has an identity element (1) and an inverse for every element but 0;
* addition and multiplication are [[commutative]] and [[associative]];
* multiplication is [[distributive property|distributive]] over addition.

Properties that are not familiar from the real numbers include:
* every element ''x'' of GF(2) satisfies {{math|1=''x'' + ''x'' = 0}} and therefore {{math|1=−''x'' = ''x''}}; this means that the [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] of GF(2) is 2;
* every element ''x'' of GF(2) satisfies {{math|1=''x''<sup>2</sup> = ''x''}} (i.e. is ''[[idempotent]]'' with respect to multiplication); this is an instance of [[Fermat's little theorem]]. GF(2) is the ''only'' field with this property (Proof: if {{math|1=''x''<sup>2</sup> = x}}, then either {{math|1=''x'' = 0}} or {{math|1=''x'' ≠ 0}}. In the latter case, ''x'' must have a multiplicative inverse, in which case dividing both sides by ''x'' gives {{math|1=''x'' = 1}}. All larger fields contain elements other than 0 and 1, and those elements cannot satisfy this property).

== Applications ==

Because of the algebraic properties above, many familiar and powerful tools of mathematics work in {{math|GF(2)}} just as well as other fields.  For example, matrix operations, including [[matrix inversion]], can be applied to matrices with elements in {{math|GF(2)}} (''see'' [[matrix ring]]).

Any [[group (mathematics)|group]] {{math|(''V'', +)}} with the property {{math|1=''v'' + ''v'' = 0}} for every {{mvar|v}} in {{mvar|V}} is necessarily [[abelian group|abelian]] and can be turned into a [[vector space]] over {{math|GF(2)}} in a natural fashion, by defining {{math|1=0''v'' = 0}} and {{math|1=1''v'' = ''v''}} for all {{mvar|v}} in {{mvar|V}}. This vector space will have a [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]], implying that the number of elements of {{mvar|V}} must be a power of 2 (or infinite). 

In modern [[computer]]s, data are represented with [[bit string]]s of a fixed length, called ''[[machine word]]s''. These are endowed with the structure of a [[vector space]] over {{math|GF(2)}}. The addition of this vector space is the [[bitwise operation]] called [[XOR]] (exclusive or). The [[bitwise AND]] is another operation on this vector space, which makes it a [[Boolean algebra (structure)|Boolean algebra]], a structure that underlies all [[computer science]]. These spaces can also be augmented with a multiplication operation that makes them into a field {{math|GF(2{{sup|''n''}})}}, but the multiplication operation cannot be a bitwise operation. When {{mvar|n}} is itself a power of two, the multiplication operation can be [[nimber|nim-multiplication]]; alternatively, for any {{mvar|n}}, one can use multiplication of polynomials over {{math|GF(2)}} modulo a [[irreducible polynomial]] (as for instance for the field {{math|GF(2{{sup|8}})}} in the description of the [[Advanced Encryption Standard]] cipher).

[[Vector space]]s and [[polynomial ring]]s over {{math|GF(2)}} are widely used in [[coding theory]], and in particular in [[error correcting code]]s and modern [[cryptography]]. For example, many common error correcting codes (such as [[BCH code]]s) are [[linear code]]s over {{math|GF(2)}} (codes defined from vector spaces over {{math|GF(2)}}), or [[polynomial code]]s (codes defined as [[quotient ring|quotients]] of polynomial rings over {{math|GF(2)}}).

== Algebraic closure ==
Like any field, GF(2) has an [[algebraic closure]]. This is a field ''F'' which contains GF(2) as a [[Field extension|subfield]], which is [[Algebraic extension|algebraic]] over GF(2) (i.e. every element of ''F'' is a root of a polynomial with coefficients in GF(2)), and which is [[Algebraically closed field|algebraically closed]] (any non-constant polynomial with coefficients in ''F'' has a root in ''F''). The field ''F'' is uniquely determined by these properties, [[up to]] a [[field automorphism]] (i.e. essentially up to the notation of its elements).

''F'' is countable and contains a single copy of each of the finite fields GF(2<sup>''n''</sup>); the copy of GF(2<sup>''n''</sup>) is contained in the copy of GF(2<sup>''m''</sup>) if and only if ''n'' divides ''m.'' The field ''F'' is countable and is the union of all these finite fields.

Conway proved that ''F'' is isomorphic to the field of ordinals below <math>\omega^{\omega^\omega}</math>, with the addition and multiplication operations defined by [[nimber addition]] and [[nimber multiplication]] respectively. <ref>{{Cite book |last=Conway |first=John H. |url= |title=On Numbers and Games |publisher= |year=2000 |isbn=978-1-56881-127-7 |edition=2nd |location=Wellesley, Mass |pages=61 |language=English}}</ref> The addition in this field is simple to perform, and [[Hendrik Lenstra|Lenstra]] has shown that the multiplication can also be performed efficiently.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lenstra |first=Hendrik |date=1977 |title=On the Algebraic Closure of Two |url=https://www.math.leidenuniv.nl/~hwl/PUBLICATIONS/1977e/art.pdf |journal=Indagationes Mathematicae (Proceedings). |volume=80 |issue=5|pages=389–396 |doi=10.1016/1385-7258(77)90053-1 }}</ref>
